Step 1 — Country-level narrowing: The scene shows right‑hand traffic, midrise plastered buildings with simple balconies, granite-like curbs, and very clean streets. Most telling are the paired overhead traction wires running down the corridor without any rail tracks, indicating trolleybuses rather than trams. Cable-suspended streetlights strung between buildings are also visible. This combination is characteristic of several Central European countries, but is notably common in Switzerland’s inner-city streets (e.g., Zürich, Bern, Lausanne, Geneva, St. Gallen), which retain extensive trolleybus networks and use catenary-suspended lamps. The overall urban tidiness and street furniture further support Switzerland over neighboring countries.

Step 2 — City-level narrowing: Among Swiss cities, the wide valley street opening toward a green, wooded hill at the end of the vista resembles Zürich’s frequent street views toward the Uetliberg ridge. Geneva’s center tends to reveal lakefront vistas; Bern’s old town streets are arcaded sandstone and more uniform; Lausanne is more steeply graded. The architecture here (postwar, plaster facades with varied balconies) and the overhead wiring pattern align well with Zürich districts outside the medieval core, suggesting Zürich rather than Bern/Lausanne/Geneva.

Step 3 — Street-level refinement: Specific features include a broad straight street with trolleybus wires centered, cable-hung luminaires mid-block, a mature tree canopy protruding on the left just before an intersection, and a distant wooded ridge aligned along the street axis. The right sidewalk has a bus-stop or kiosk-like shelter and a distinctive high curb with rounded gutter. This combination of a trolleybus corridor pointing toward the ridge and the left-side large roadside tree narrows to a typical Zürich neighborhood arterial rather than a purely commercial boulevard or lakeside quay.
